Key documented facts:
- No visa/entry/border condition targeting LGBTQ travellers; but general ID-carry rule at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, fines up to 3,000, detention warnings. This is a universal-exposure document-check mechanism that initiates police contact — relevant for trans visitors.
- Aug 2025: ~20 trans women stopped and detained at a police station, released after "general information gathering" background checks — documented targeting of trans people in public space (street, shops, cafés) in a central district. This is tier 2: state-tolerated/state-directed targeting — police profiling of trans women, documentation without charge.
- 313 violations in 2025, 2.5x 2024; 299 detention decisions (256 recorded, 43 off record); systematic privacy attacks. Note: this is an LGBTI+ aggregate, not trans-specific — per rule 17, an LGBT-wide figure. But detention dominance and trans-disproportionate effect noted in Feb 2026 report: six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings; transgender individuals disproportionately affected.
- Draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague "family"/"public morals" claims — not established as enacted. Also considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with 1-3 years — NOT included in 2026 judicial package. So no criminalisation of trans identity in force; threat is drift.
- No comprehensive anti-discrimination law, no gender-identity protection. Resident-facing gap.
- Prison conditions: segregation/isolation, arbitrary strip searches, solitary confinement with restricted healthcare, no policy or training, complaints ineffective and can lead to further violence. Trans man held in women's prison. Poyraz found dead in cell at women's prison 1 Dec 2025, with delayed medical response, investigators arriving two days later, no witness statements taken. This is custody exposure — relevant if a visitor is detained. Severity 4-5 in custody. But how likely is a visitor to end in prison? Low; short police holding conditions not sourced (the Aug 2025 detentions were station holds, released).
- Violence: trans woman Yaşam knifed Aug 2024; perpetrator released while victim referred for arrest — detention asymmetry. Six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence 2025, three hate killings (national scale). Background: not trans-specific rate given denominators; this is a country with substantial population. Per rule 16, need background rate; six deaths including three hate killings across a whole country for LGBTI+ is roughly in line with background or elevated but not a campaign.
- Pride monitoring: entrenched discrimination, senior officials' rhetoric deepening transphobia.
- Health: HRT not covered by government healthcare — visitors must pay privately; sex reassignment surgery available at 18 in major cities; state hospital required for marker change. For a visitor needing medication continuity, must arrange privately — friction but not denial of emergency care. Sept 2025 regulation: "gender reassignment" added to medical-board reporting reasons; hospitals barred from "other" option, e-reports — profiling risk in healthcare settings for trans people, though largely resident-facing (marker change), but medical-board reporting could touch a visitor seeking care.
- Sept 2026 raids: 162 suspects, 9 associations, 13 businesses under investigation, framed as protecting children. Recent (Sept 2026) state enforcement action against LGBTQ+ organisations — shows escalation, though resident-facing.
- April 2026: city LGBTI+ group ordered dissolved, 11 founders on trial; broadcasting regulator fining platforms. State threat-framing.
- 2019: police broke up student Pride, 25 arrests.
- Public opinion dated (2020 or earlier), 25% national acceptance of homosexuality.

Now the combined regime: no subnational divergence documented as protective; city-marked geography only. So national regime.

Worst documented feature: police profiling/street stops and detention of trans women for ID/background checks — tier 2 (state-tolerated or state-directed targeting: police profiling, documentation, "general information gathering"), plus in custody severe conditions (tier 1-ish for custody but conditional on being detained). Also a general ID-carry checkpoint rule that reaches every visitor in holiday destinations — universal exposure mechanism, though detection is discretionary and ID check may not out a trans visitor whose passport matches presentation... but a mismatch (marker vs presentation) triggers.

No criminalisation of trans identity in force. Legislative drift risk (unresolved whether draft enacted). So not a 0.15 tier.

Compare anchors:
- 0.35-B (Karthovia): police stop trans visitors, confiscate passports/phones, compel lengthy interviews, release after hours, sometimes fines under vague bylaw; courts defer. That is quite similar to the August 2025 street stops, though here it was ~20 trans women residents (not documented visitors) released after background checks. But here the surrounding conditions are worse: prison conditions documented as abusive with a death, official rhetoric hostile, escalating legislative/associational crackdown, no anti-discrimination protection, a documented killing with detention asymmetry, and a general ID-check regime. So above 0.35 in severity? Wait higher score = safer. So this jurisdiction should be BELOW 0.35-B probably.

- 0.25 anchors: 0.25-A (Varnalia): police raids on trans centre, visitors detained, photographed, released after fines, officers demand payments; courts overturn some; imprisonment rare; execution not imposed. Similar tier. 0.25-C (Ostravia): prison housing by birth sex with assaults frequent; statute criminalizes cross-dressing in administrative buildings; courts recognize right in principle but slow; brief sentences; no capital. 0.25-D (Caldera): morality provision applied selectively, undercover entrapment, blackmail; appellate judges annul some; fines and short jail terms; capital not applicable.

Our dossier: no statute criminalising cross-dressing or public indecency applied to gender presentation documented (the "behaviour contrary to biological sex" advocacy provision wasn't included). Police detention under general background-check powers. No documented extortion/bribery pattern. So arguably somewhat better than 0.25-A/D in legal exposure; but worse in custody severity (a death in custody, strip searches, isolation) and in state threat-framing (draft criminalisation package, raids on associations, official rhetoric). Hmm.

- Low probability of border/entry friction (no trans-specific entry rules documented; absence of evidence, but in a well-documented state silence on airport screening is a mildly positive signal — though the dossier explicitly says "Deliberately not counted" for airport screening, so it's genuinely uncertain/no conclusion).
- Real risk of street police stop and detention if visibly trans in a major city central district. Documented targeting of trans women specifically. That's a traveler-facing exposure: visitors present in those districts.
- If detained in custody longer-term: severe, tier 4-ish (documented death, solitary, strip searches).
- Street violence: hate killings documented at national scale, detention asymmetry for a trans victim.
- Healthcare: private-only HRT continuity; profiling risk through medical-board reporting.

I'd say ours is comparable-to-slightly-worse than 0.25-C. Perhaps 0.22-0.25.
